q: XSS needs two things to go wrong at the same time. Which pair?
options: The server responds slowly, and the user chose a weak password
The site runs over plain HTTP, and the user is on public WiFi
The page takes in text it did not write (user input, URL, API response), and puts it into the DOM without escaping or sanitizing it
The page loads many third-party scripts, and one of them fails to load
explain: Untrusted text AND no escaping — both must be true. Untrusted text that gets escaped is harmless, and escaping only matters for text that came from outside. When both line up, the browser cannot tell the attacker's markup from yours: it runs on your origin, so it can read the page, read any cookie your JS can read, and send requests as the logged-in user. The other options are real problems (weak passwords, plain HTTP, a flaky CDN) but none of them put attacker text into your page.

q: React's JSX escapes the values you insert. Where does that protection stop?
options: It only covers values rendered as text. Values used as an attribute, a URL (href/src), an inline style, or passed to dangerouslySetInnerHTML are not made safe
It does not stop — JSX makes every value safe in every position
It stops for numbers; only strings get escaped
It only runs in development builds; production builds skip it for speed
explain:
JSX escapes text nodes, so

{userInput}

is safe. It does not understand where the value lands: still accepts "javascript:alert(1)", a style value can smuggle a url(), and dangerouslySetInnerHTML turns escaping off entirely — that is what the name is warning you about. Escaping is per-context: HTML text, HTML attribute, URL and CSS each have different rules, and one escaper cannot cover all four.

q: You genuinely need to render raw HTML that came from a user. What do you reach for?

Nothing special — React escapes it for you, even inside dangerouslySetInnerHTML
Base64-encode the string and decode it in the browser
A maintained HTML sanitizer such as DOMPurify, run on the value before you render it

q: What is a Content Security Policy actually for?
options: Stopping XSS bugs from being written into your code in the first place
Limiting what injected code can do when an XSS bug does get through
Encrypting traffic between the browser and the server
Checking who the user is before letting them in
explain: CSP is a header telling the browser which scripts, styles and connections this page is allowed to run and make. It cannot stop you from writing an injection bug — the attacker's string still reaches the page — but it can stop that string from executing, and stop it from sending stolen data anywhere. Encrypting traffic is HTTPS's job; identifying users is authentication's job. CSP is damage control that sits behind sanitizing, never instead of it.

q: Why is an allowlist CSP (listing approved domains in script-src) a poor bet?
options: Browsers quietly ignore allowlists and only honour nonces
Allowlists only take effect over HTTP, not HTTPS
Allowing a whole domain trusts everything on it — one old library or open JSONP endpoint there defeats the policy — and the list rots every time a vendor changes a hostname
Allowlists noticeably slow the page down
explain: An allowlist says "any script from this CDN is fine". Large-scale studies of real sites found most allowlist policies bypassable, usually through a JSONP endpoint or an outdated framework already hosted on an allowed domain — and keeping the list accurate is endless work. A strict CSP trusts a per-response nonce (or a hash) that an attacker cannot guess, and 'strict-dynamic' lets your trusted scripts load their own. As a bonus it also blocks inline event handlers, eval(), object embeds and <base> tag hijacking.

q: What is the first step when rolling out a strict CSP?
options: Enforce the strict policy in production and fix whatever breaks
Add 'unsafe-inline' first so nothing breaks, and remove it later
Remove every third-party script from the site
Ship it as Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only and collect the violation reports
explain: Report-Only evaluates the exact same policy and reports every violation, but blocks nothing — so you find out what would break before a single user does. Enforcing first breaks production instead. Adding 'unsafe-inline' ships a policy that does nothing against XSS, and "remove it later" rarely happens. Removing all third-party scripts is not a CSP step at all. Order: Report-Only → fix the inline handlers it flags and add nonces or hashes → add 'strict-dynamic' where scripts load scripts → enforce.

q: Which of these should never appear in your CSP?
options: 'unsafe-inline' in script-src
A nonce generated fresh for every response
default-src https: as a baseline fallback
'strict-dynamic'
explain: 'unsafe-inline' permits any inline <script> and any on* handler — which is precisely the shape of an XSS payload, so the policy stops defending against the thing it exists for. A fresh per-response nonce and 'strict-dynamic' are the two building blocks of a strict policy, and default-src https: is weak but harmless as a baseline when a strict policy is not realistic yet. Avoid data: in script-src and wildcard sources for the same reason as 'unsafe-inline': they let attacker-supplied code qualify as allowed code.

q: Your JS bundle is public. Which of these counts as information leakage?
options: Only hardcoded passwords
Only a source map you published by accident
Hardcoded credentials, API keys with no restrictions on them, and internal or admin URLs and endpoints left in the code
Nothing — the bundle is minified
explain: Anything the browser downloads is readable by anyone who opens devtools, so it is all public by definition. Credentials are the obvious loss; an unrestricted API key is someone else's bill and someone else's data; and internal or admin endpoints are a free map of where to attack next, even if they are access-controlled. Passwords and source maps are two items on that list, not the whole list. Keep secrets on the server, restrict any key that must ship (by referrer, IP or API scope), and grep production bundles for them on a schedule.

q: Does minifying your JavaScript hide what is inside it?
options: Yes — minified code is unreadable
No — your logic, strings, URLs and endpoint paths all survive intact; minifying only shortens local names and strips whitespace
Yes, as long as you gzip the bundle as well
Yes, once you turn source maps off
explain: Minifying is a size optimisation, not a protection. Every string literal, URL, API path and branch of your logic is still in the file, and devtools will pretty-print it back into readable code in one click. Gzip is transport compression and changes nothing once the browser unpacks it. Turning off source maps only removes the convenience of original names and comments. Decide on purpose whether .js.map files ship publicly or get uploaded privately to a tool like Sentry — then check whether yours are already sitting next to the bundle in production.

q: An attacker's page makes your logged-in user's browser send a real request your user never intended. What stops it?
options: A stricter Content Security Policy
A correctly configured CORS policy
Minifying the bundle
A CSRF token the attacker's page cannot read, plus SameSite cookies
explain: The browser attaches your cookies to that cross-site request automatically, so the server sees a perfectly valid call from a logged-in user. A CSRF token works because the attacker's page cannot read a value out of your page to include it, and SameSite=Lax or Strict stops the cookie from riding along at all. CORS does not help here: it governs whether the attacker may read the response, but the write has already happened. CSP and minification are unrelated to this attack.

q: Where should an auth token live?
options: In localStorage, so your JavaScript can read it and attach it to requests
In an httpOnly cookie, which JavaScript cannot read at all — paired with Secure and SameSite
In sessionStorage, since it clears when the tab closes
In the URL, so it survives a page refresh
explain: Anything your JavaScript can read, injected JavaScript can read too — one XSS and the token is exfiltrated. sessionStorage is no safer than localStorage on this point; it only shortens the window. httpOnly keeps the token out of JS entirely, Secure keeps it off plain HTTP, and SameSite covers the CSRF risk that cookies otherwise bring. Tokens in URLs are the worst case: they leak through browser history, Referer headers, server logs and anything the user copy-pastes.

q: The Delete button is hidden for users without permission. Is the action protected?
options: No — hiding a button only changes the UI; the server has to check permission on the request itself
Yes — if they cannot see the button, they cannot trigger the action
Yes, as long as the route is hidden from the router too
Yes, as long as the site is served over HTTPS
explain: The button, the router and the entire bundle run on the user's machine, so all of it can be edited, and curl or Postman never loads your UI in the first place — the endpoint is one request away regardless. The only check that counts is the server-side one, for that specific user against that specific record, on every call. HTTPS protects the request in transit; it says nothing about who is allowed to make it.

q: Which CORS setup is the dangerous one?
options: Allowing one specific trusted origin
Allowing your own origin only
Reflecting back whatever Origin arrived (or using *) while also allowing credentials
Blocking all cross-origin reads
explain: Allowing any origin together with credentials means any website your user visits can call your API as that logged-in user and read the response. Browsers reject a literal '*' when credentials are allowed, so this usually shows up as a server echoing the request's Origin header straight back — same hole, harder to spot in a config review. Allow an explicit list of origins you control. Blocking cross-origin reads is the browser's safe default, not a risk.

q: A user edits an ID in the URL and sees someone else's data. Where is the bug?
options: In the frontend router, for letting the ID be edited
In the CORS configuration
In using a sequential ID instead of an unguessable one
On the server — it returned the record without checking that this user is allowed to see it
explain: This is IDOR (insecure direct object reference). Every value in a URL is attacker-controlled, so the server must answer "is this user allowed to touch this record?" and not only "does this record exist?". A random UUID just makes IDs harder to guess — the link still works for anyone who obtains one, so that is obscurity, not authorization. The router is frontend UI and CORS governs cross-origin reads; neither one ever makes a permission decision.

q: Your login page accepts any URL in ?redirect=. What is the risk?
options: Your trusted domain becomes the first hop of a phishing chain, bouncing users to a lookalike login page
The session cookie gets copied into the redirect parameter
It breaks CORS preflight requests
It makes the redirect slower
explain: Users and mail filters judge the domain they can see, and that domain really is yours — the attacker's URL is hidden in the parameter, and the victim lands on a copy of your login form already trusting it. The same bug is used to steal OAuth codes when the redirect target is not pinned. Fix it by validating the target against an allowlist, or by accepting only relative paths — and reject "//evil.com", which looks relative but the browser reads as a protocol-relative absolute URL.

q: Most of a modern frontend is code you did not write. How does risk get in?
options: Only through packages you chose and installed yourself
Through hijacked or compromised packages, typosquatted names, and transitive dependencies you never chose to install
Only through devDependencies, which never ship to users
It does not — the registry reviews every package before publishing
explain: npm publishes whatever is uploaded; nobody reviews it on your behalf. Most of your dependency tree consists of packages you never picked, pulled in by the ones you did, and a single maintainer-account takeover turns a trusted name malicious in one version. devDependencies are not safe either — they execute on developer machines and in CI, which is where the deploy tokens live. Pin with a committed lockfile, install with npm ci, run audit or a scanner in CI, and keep the tree as small as the job allows.
